q-130263.name: Question 1
q-130263.problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy$ at the point $(1,1)$ in the direction of the vector $v=i-j.$
q-130263.worked_solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}=\sqrt{2} \\ u & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i-j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy)j \\  & =(2x-y)\,i+(2y-x)\,j \\ ∇\,f(1,1) & =(2(1)-1)\,i+(2(1)-1)\,j \\  & =i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(1,1) & =∇\,f(1,1)\cdot u \\  & =(i+j)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i-j) \\  & =\frac{1(1)+1(-1)}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

q-36306.name: Question 2
q-36306.problem:
Given the function  $g(x,y)=({x}^{2}+y)^{2}$, find its directional derivative at the
point $A(-1,1)$ in the direction that's towards the point $B(3,4).$
q-36306.worked_solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the direction vector and the corresponding unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨3,4⟩-⟨-1,1⟩ \\  & =⟨4,3⟩ \\ u & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}}{‖\overset{\to }{AB}‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{4}^{2}}}⟨4,3⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨4,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the gradient $∇g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $A(-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+y)^{2},\,\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+y)^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨4x({x}^{2}+y),\,2({x}^{2}+y)⟩ \\ ∇g(-1,1) & =⟨4\cdot (-1)\cdot ((-1)^{2}+1),2\cdot ((-1)^{2}+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-8,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{u}^{′}(-1,1) & =∇g(-1,1)\cdot u \\  & =⟨-8,4⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{4}{5},\frac{3}{5}⟩ \\  & =-8\cdot \frac{4}{5}+4\cdot \frac{3}{5} \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

q-130268.problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ at the point $A(4,3)$ in the direction towards the point $B(1,1).$
q-130268.worked_solution:
The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the direction vector and the corresponding unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨1,1⟩-⟨4,3⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,-2⟩ \\ u & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}}{‖\overset{\to }{AB}‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+(-2)^{2}}}⟨-3,-2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}⟨-3,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $A(4,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}},\,\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}⟩ \\ ∇f(4,3) & =⟨\frac{4}{\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{3}^{2}}},\,\frac{3}{\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{3}^{2}}}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{4}{5},\frac{3}{5}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(4,3) & =∇f(4,3)\cdot u \\  & =⟨\frac{4}{5},\frac{3}{5}⟩\cdot ⟨-\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}},-\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}⟩ \\  & =\frac{4(-3)+3(-2)}{5\sqrt{13}} \\  & =-\frac{18}{5\sqrt{13}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

$$

q-36293.problem: In what direction does the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{x}^{2}y$ increase most rapidly at the point $(1,1)?$
q-36293.worked_solution:
At a given point, a function $f(x,y)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

So, we compute $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{x}^{2}y)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{x}^{2}y)\text{ }j \\  & =(2xy-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\text{ }i+{x}^{2}\text{ }j \\ ∇f(1,1) & =(2\cdot 1\cdot 1-\operatorname{sin}⁡(1))\text{ }i+{1}^{2}\text{ }j \\  & =(2-\operatorname{sin}⁡(1))\text{ }i+j\end{aligned}

q-36293.html:
Question 6
?

In what direction does the function f(x,y)=cos⁡x+x2y increase most rapidly at the point (1,1)?

a
−2i−j
b
2i+j
c
(sin⁡(1)−2)i−j
d
(2−sin⁡(1))i+j
e
−sin⁡(1)i+2j
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

At a given point, a function f(x,y) increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

So, we compute ∇f(x,y) and evaluate it at the point (1,1):

∇f(x,y)=∂∂x(cos⁡x+x2y) i+∂∂y(cos⁡x+x2y) j=(2xy−sin⁡x) i+x2 j∇f(1,1)=(2⋅1⋅1−sin⁡(1)) i+12 j=(2−sin⁡(1)) i+j

Therefore, the function increases most rapidly in the direction of (2−sin⁡(1))i+j.

q-86539.problem: In what direction does the function $g(x,y,z)={e}^{xy}+3{z}^{2}y$ increase most rapidly at the point $(2,2,-1)?$
q-86539.worked_solution:
At a given point, a function $g(x,y,z)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

So, we compute $∇g(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at the point $(2,2,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y,z) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{xy}+3{z}^{2}y),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{xy}+3{z}^{2}y),\,\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{xy}+3{z}^{2}y)⟩ \\  & =⟨y{e}^{xy},\,x{e}^{xy}+3{z}^{2},\,6yz⟩ \\ ∇g(2,2,-1) & =⟨2\cdot {e}^{2\cdot 2},\,2\cdot {e}^{2\cdot 2}+3(-1)^{2},\,6\cdot 2\cdot (-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2{e}^{4},\,2{e}^{4}+3,\,-12⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function increases most rapidly in the direction of $⟨2{e}^{4},\,2{e}^{4}+3,\,-12⟩.$

Question 7
?

In what direction does the function g(x,y,z)=exy+3z2y increase most rapidly at the point (2,2,−1)?

a
⟨4e2,2e4−3,−12⟩
b
⟨2e4,2e4+3,−12⟩
c
⟨2e4,2e−3,−21⟩
d
⟨2e,e4−3,12⟩
e
⟨2e4,2e2+3,12⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

At a given point, a function g(x,y,z) increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

So, we compute ∇g(x,y,z) and evaluate it at the point (2,2,−1):

∇g(x,y,z)=⟨∂∂x(exy+3z2y),∂∂y(exy+3z2y),∂∂z(exy+3z2y)⟩=⟨yexy,xexy+3z2,6yz⟩∇g(2,2,−1)=⟨2⋅e2⋅2,2⋅e2⋅2+3(−1)2,6⋅2⋅(−1)⟩=⟨2e4,2e4+3,−12⟩

Therefore, the function increases most rapidly in the direction of ⟨2e4,2e4+3,−12⟩.

q-83598.name: Question 8
q-83598.problem: In what direction does the function $g(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+z)$ decrease most rapidly at the point $(1,1,1)?$
q-83598.worked_solution:
At a given point, a function $g(x,y,z)$ decreases most rapidly in the direction opposite to that of its gradient.

So, we compute $-∇g(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}-∇g(x,y,z) & =-⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}+4\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+z)),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}+4\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+z)),\,\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{y}^{2}+4\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+z))⟩ \\  & =-⟨{y}^{2}-\frac{4}{x+z},\,2xy,\,-\frac{4}{x+z}⟩ \\ -∇g(1,1,1) & =-⟨{1}^{2}-\frac{4}{1+1},\,2\cdot 1\cdot 1,\,-\frac{4}{1+1}⟩ \\  & =-⟨-1,\,2,\,-2⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-2,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function decreases most rapidly in the direction of $⟨1,\,-2,\,2⟩.$

In what direction does the function g(x,y,z)=xy2−4ln⁡(x+z) decrease most rapidly at the point (1,1,1)?

a
 ⟨−1,2,−2⟩
b
 ⟨−3,−4,4⟩
c
 ⟨3,4,−4⟩
d
 ⟨1,−2,2⟩
e
 ⟨0,−2,1⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

At a given point, a function g(x,y,z) decreases most rapidly in the direction opposite to that of its gradient.

So, we compute −∇g(x,y,z) and evaluate it at the point (1,1,1):

−∇g(x,y,z)=−⟨∂∂x(xy2+4ln⁡(x+z)),∂∂y(xy2+4ln⁡(x+z)),∂∂z(xy2+4ln⁡(x+z))⟩=−⟨y2−4x+z,2xy,−4x+z⟩−∇g(1,1,1)=−⟨12−41+1,2⋅1⋅1,−41+1⟩=−⟨−1,2,−2⟩=⟨1,−2,2⟩

Therefore, the function decreases most rapidly in the direction of ⟨1,−2,2⟩.

q-130273.problem: In what direction does the function $g(x,y,z)=10-3{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-{z}^{3}$ increase most rapidly at the point $(1,-\frac{1}{2},-1)?$
q-130273.worked_solution:
At a given point, a function $g(x,y,z)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

So, we compute $∇g(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,-\frac{1}{2},-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y,z) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(10-3{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-{z}^{3}),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(10-3{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-{z}^{3}),\,\frac{∂}{∂z}(10-3{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-{z}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨-6x,\,-2y,\,-3{z}^{2}⟩ \\ ∇g(1,-\frac{1}{2},-1) & =⟨-6(1),-2(-\frac{1}{2}),-3(-1)^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-6,1,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

In what direction does the function g(x,y,z)=10−3x2−y2−z3 increase most rapidly at the point (1,−12,−1)?

a
⟨−3,2,1⟩
b
⟨0,2,−4⟩
c
⟨−6,1,−3⟩
d
⟨1,−1,4⟩
e
⟨−2,−5,0⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

At a given point, a function g(x,y,z) increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

So, we compute ∇g(x,y,z) and evaluate it at the point (1,−12,−1): ∇g(x,y,z)=⟨∂∂x(10−3x2−y2−z3),∂∂y(10−3x2−y2−z3),∂∂z(10−3x2−y2−z3)⟩=⟨−6x,−2y,−3z2⟩∇g(1,−12,−1)=⟨−6(1),−2(−12),−3(−1)2⟩=⟨−6,1,−3⟩

Therefore, the function increases most rapidly in the direction of ⟨−6,1,−3⟩.

q-83554.name: Question 10
q-83554.problem: In what direction does the function $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+y{e}^{x}-xy$ increase most rapidly at the point $(-1,1)?$
q-83554.worked_solution:
At a given point, a function $f(x,y)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

So, we compute $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+y{e}^{x}-xy)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+y{e}^{x}-xy)\text{ }j \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡y+y{e}^{x}-y)\text{ }i+(\frac{x}{y}+{e}^{x}-x)\text{ }j \\ ∇f(1,1) & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡1+1\cdot {e}^{-1}-1)\text{ }i+(\frac{-1}{1}+{e}^{-1}-(-1))\text{ }j \\  & =({e}^{-1}-1)\text{ }i+{e}^{-1}j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function increases most rapidly in the direction of $({e}^{-1}-1)\text{ }i+{e}^{-1}j.$

So, we compute ∇f(x,y) and evaluate it at the point (−1,1):

∇f(x,y)=∂∂x(xln⁡y+yex−xy) i+∂∂y(xln⁡y+yex−xy) j=(ln⁡y+yex−y) i+(xy+ex−x) j∇f(1,1)=(ln⁡1+1⋅e−1−1) i+(−11+e−1−(−1)) j=(e−1−1) i+e−1j

q-83609.name: Question 11
q-83609.problem: Consider the function $g(x,y)=xy{e}^{x+y}+{x}^{2}y.$ What is the rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(1,-1)$ in the direction of the vector $v=⟨3,-4⟩?$
q-83609.worked_solution:
The rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(1,-1)$ in the direction of $v$ is equal to the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(1,-1).$ 

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+(-4)^{2}}=\sqrt{25}=5 \\ u & =\frac{1}{5}⟨3,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the gradient $∇\,g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy{e}^{x+y}+{x}^{2}y),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy{e}^{x+y}+{x}^{2}y)⟩ \\  & =⟨y{e}^{x+y}+xy{e}^{x+y}+2xy,\,x{e}^{x+y}+xy{e}^{x+y}+{x}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨y(1+x){e}^{x+y}+2xy,\,x(1+y){e}^{x+y}+{x}^{2}⟩ \\ ∇\,g(1,-1) & =⟨(-1)\cdot (1+1){e}^{1-1}+2\cdot 1\cdot (-1),\,1\cdot (1-1){e}^{1-1}+{1}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-4,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(1,-1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{u}^{′}(1,-1) & =∇\,g(1,1)\cdot u \\  & =⟨-4,1⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{3}{5},-\frac{4}{5}⟩ \\  & =\frac{(-4)\cdot 3+1\cdot (-4)}{5} \\  & =-\frac{16}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-130806.problem: Consider the function $g(x,y)={x}^{y}.$ What is the rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(1,1)$ in the direction in which the function increases most rapidly?
q-130806.worked_solution:
At a given point, a function $g(x,y)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

In our case, we compute $∇g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{y}),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{y})⟩ \\  & =⟨y{x}^{y-1},\,{x}^{y}\operatorname{ln}⁡x⟩ \\ ∇\,g(1,1) & =⟨(1){1}^{1-1},\,({1}^{1})\operatorname{ln}⁡1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(1,1)$ in the direction of $∇g(1,1)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}‖∇\,g(1,1)‖ & =‖⟨1,0⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

q-130804.name: Question 13
q-130804.problem: Consider the function $g(x,y)=4{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}.$ What is the rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(2,1)$ in the direction of the vector $v=⟨5,12⟩?$
q-130804.worked_solution:
The rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(2,1)$ in the direction of $v$ is equal to the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(2,1).$ 

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{5}^{2}+{12}^{2}}=13 \\ u & =\frac{1}{13}⟨5,12⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the gradient $∇g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(4{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨8x,\,-6y⟩ \\ ∇g(2,1) & =⟨8(2),-6(1)⟩ \\  & =⟨16,-6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(2,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{u}^{′}(2,1) & =∇g(2,1)\cdot u \\  & =⟨16,-6⟩\cdot \frac{1}{13}⟨5,12⟩ \\  & =\frac{16(5)-6(12)}{13} \\  & =\frac{80-72}{13} \\  & =\frac{8}{13}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-130811.problem: Consider the function $f(x,y)=2\sqrt{xy}.$ What is the rate of change of $f(x,y)$ at the point $(8,2)$ in the direction in which the function decreases most rapidly?
q-130811.worked_solution:
At a given point, a function $f(x,y)$ decreases most rapidly in the opposite direction of its gradient at that point.

In our case, we compute $-∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(8,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}-∇f(x,y) & =-\frac{∂}{∂x}(2\sqrt{xy})i-\frac{∂}{∂y}(2\sqrt{xy})j \\  & =-\sqrt{\frac{y}{x}}\,i-\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}}\,j \\ -∇f(8,2) & =-\sqrt{\frac{2}{8}}\,i-\sqrt{\frac{8}{2}}\,j \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\,i-2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the rate of change of $f(x,y)$ at the point $(8,2)$ in the direction of $-∇f(8,2)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}‖-∇f(8,2)‖ & =‖-\frac{1}{2}\,i-2\,j‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+(-2)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}+4} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{17}{4}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{17}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-37074.problem: Consider the function $g(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x).$ What is the rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(e,\pi )$ in the direction in which the function increases most rapidly?
q-37074.worked_solution:
At a given point, a function $g(x,y)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

In our case, we compute $∇g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(e,\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x))⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\cdot \frac{y}{x},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡x⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{y\operatorname{cos}⁡(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{x},\,\operatorname{ln}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x)⟩ \\ ∇\,g(e,\pi ) & =⟨\frac{\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \operatorname{ln}⁡e)}{e},\,\operatorname{ln}⁡e\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \operatorname{ln}⁡e)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi }{e},\,1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\pi \cdot (-1)}{e},\,1\cdot (-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{\pi }{e},\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(e,\pi )$ in the direction of $∇g(e,\pi )$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}‖∇\,g(e,\pi )‖ & =‖⟨-\frac{\pi }{e},-1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{{e}^{2}}+1} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{\pi }^{2}+{e}^{2}}}{e}\end{aligned}
$$
